chapters.title: The model only sees the score

items.title: Last time, we said a model is a machine with knobs
items.subtitle: Last time, we said a model is a machine with knobs, and learning means turning those knobs to the right spot.

items.title: But what does "right" even mean?
items.subtitle: But what does "right" even mean? How does the machine know this turn beat the last one?

items.title: The trick is to give its mistakes a score.
items.subtitle: The trick is to give its mistakes a score.

items.title: That score is called the loss
items.subtitle: That score is called the loss, and the rule for working it out is the loss function. That's today's topic.

items.title: Every time the model guesses
items.subtitle: Every time the model guesses, it lands a bit too high or too low. That gap is the error.

items.title: Roll all those errors up into one number
items.subtitle: Roll all those errors up into one number, and that's the loss: a score for how wrong it is.

items.title: It's the opposite of a test score:
items.subtitle: It's the opposite of a test score: lower is better, and zero means not wrong at all.

items.title: Kind of like golf
items.subtitle: Kind of like golf, where fewer strokes is better.

items.title: Now the machine can check itself.
items.subtitle: Now the machine can check itself. If a turn lowers the score, keep it. If not, turn it back.

items.title: So training is just turning the knobs
items.subtitle: So training is just turning the knobs again and again to push that score down.

items.title: Remember those twelve made-up taxi rides?
items.subtitle: Remember those twelve made-up taxi rides? Distance along the bottom, fare up the side.

items.title: The model's still that straight line
items.subtitle: The model's still that straight line, with two knobs: starting fare and price per kilometer.

items.title: First try: a $5 starting fare and $2 a kilometer.
items.subtitle: First try: a $5 starting fare and $2 a kilometer. The whole line sits too low.

items.title: Take the 5-kilometer ride:
items.subtitle: Take the 5-kilometer ride: it cost $23, the model guessed $15, so it's off by $8. That's the error.

items.title: Now square it:
items.subtitle: Now square it: eight times eight is 64. That's the red square.

items.title: Do that for all twelve rides
items.subtitle: Do that for all twelve rides, take the average, and this setting scores 78.

items.title: Second try: $4 to start and $3.50 a kilometer.
items.subtitle: Second try: $4 to start and $3.50 a kilometer. Too steep, so short rides come out low and long ones high.

items.title: If we skip the squaring
items.subtitle: If we skip the squaring and just average the errors, the lows and the highs cancel out.

items.title: The average is only −$0.33
items.subtitle: The average is only −$0.33, so it looks like it's barely wrong at all.

items.title: So we square.
items.subtitle: So we square. Everything turns positive, and nothing cancels.

items.title: And big misses cost way more:
items.subtitle: And big misses cost way more: off by two costs four, but off by eight costs 64.

items.title: Square, then average
items.subtitle: Square, then average, and this setting scores 13.4.

items.title: This is called mean squared error
items.subtitle: This is called mean squared error, and it's one of the most common loss functions.

items.title: Third try: $10 to start, $2.50 a kilometer.
items.subtitle: Third try: $10 to start, $2.50 a kilometer. The squares are tiny, and it scores 2.19.

items.title: The third has the lowest score
items.subtitle: The third has the lowest score, so it's the best of the three.

items.title: But that's only three tries.
items.subtitle: But that's only three tries. Score every setting of both knobs, and you get a landscape of scores.

items.title: Starting fare along the bottom
items.subtitle: Starting fare along the bottom, price per kilometer up the side, and the darker the color, the higher the score.

items.title: Our three tries:
items.subtitle: Our three tries: the first way up high, the second halfway down, the third nearly at the bottom of the valley.

items.title: The best is $10.20 to start
items.subtitle: The best is $10.20 to start and $2.54 a kilometer. It scores 1.97.

items.title: It's the best setting
items.subtitle: It's the best setting, and the whole job of training is finding that lowest point.

items.title: Here's something easy to miss:
items.subtitle: Here's something easy to miss: even the lowest point isn't zero.

items.title: Real fares bounce around
items.subtitle: Real fares bounce around with traffic and detours, so no straight line could nail every ride.

items.title: Training isn't chasing zero.
items.subtitle: Training isn't chasing zero. It's getting as low as it can.

items.title: Here's the thing:
items.subtitle: Here's the thing: the model has no idea what a taxi is. All it sees is the score.

items.title: The way you score it shapes how it learns.
items.subtitle: The way you score it shapes how it learns. Because we squared the errors, it's terrified of big mistakes.

items.title: It would rather be a little off
items.subtitle: It would rather be a little off on every ride than way off on just one.

items.title: So when you pick a loss function
items.subtitle: So when you pick a loss function, you're really telling the model what "good" means.

items.title: Big language models like ChatGPT
items.subtitle: Big language models like ChatGPT get a score in training too, just not for taxi fares.

items.title: Their job is to guess the next word
items.subtitle: Their job is to guess the next word, like what comes after "Twinkle, twinkle, little."

items.title: The score checks how sure the model
items.subtitle: The score checks how sure the model was about the real next word. The less sure, the bigger the penalty.

items.title: If it was 90% sure of the right word
items.subtitle: If it was 90% sure of the right word, the penalty's tiny. Only 10% sure, and it's way bigger.

items.title: This kind of scoring
items.subtitle: This kind of scoring is called cross-entropy. The name is all you need for now.

items.title: In 2023, Meta tracked that score while
items.subtitle: In 2023, Meta tracked that score while training a model called Llama 2.

items.title: It read 2 trillion tokens of text.
items.subtitle: It read 2 trillion tokens of text. Tokens are roughly words or bits of words.

items.title: And even then
items.subtitle: And even then, the score was still falling, nowhere near flat.

items.title: A big model has tens of billions of knobs
items.subtitle: A big model has tens of billions of knobs, we have two, but the job's the same: find the lowest point.

items.title: So, a loss function is how
items.subtitle: So, a loss function is how you score the model's mistakes, and lower is better.

items.title: And training is just
items.subtitle: And training is just pushing that score down.

items.title: But with tons of knobs
items.subtitle: But with tons of knobs, that landscape's way too big to see all at once. So which way do you turn to go downhill?

items.title: That's where gradient descent comes in.
items.subtitle: That's where gradient descent comes in. It's up next time.
